title: The Ants Get Ready for Winter
theme: Getting ready for winter, counting and helping each other
blurb: Patter the ant has to carry seven grains of wheat to the nest before the rain comes. On the way she helps Dotty the ladybird, whose wings are wet with dew; then the ants carry, Dotty counts, and nobody is left alone in the rain.

pages.text: Autumn had come. Yellow leaves fell, rustle rustle. Patter the ant lived under the old log. She waggled her antennae: “It's getting chilly. Winter is coming! I must carry seven grains of wheat to the nest.”
pages.ask: How do we know autumn has come? What can you see outside?

pages.text: Patter found grains of wheat in the meadow. Grey clouds were gathering in the sky. Patter got in a flap. Her heart went thump, thump. She took a deep breath. “I need seven. How many are here? Let's count first.”

pitir.say: I must finish before the rain!

mech.done: Seven grains of wheat! You counted them all.

pages.ask: Can you show seven with your fingers? Was one hand enough?

pages.text: Patter lifted the first grain onto her head. Heave, ho! It was so heavy. But she didn't give up. “Step by step, one more step!” A thin little voice came from the grass. It was Dotty the ladybird. She sniffed: “My wings are wet with dew, I can't fly!”

pitir.say: Heave! Step by step, one more step!

benek.say: My wings are wet, I can't go buzz!

predict.q: What do you think Patter will do?
predict.res: Both are good ideas! Let's see.

pages.ask: Why can't Dotty fly? How do you think she feels now?

pages.text: The clouds were getting closer, but Patter put the grain down. “Come, Dotty, let's walk to that sunny spot. Your wings will dry in the sun.” Step by step, one more step!

mech.done: Dotty reached the sun. Ahh, nice and warm!

pages.ask: Why did Patter put the grain down to help Dotty? Have you ever helped a friend?

pages.text: In the sun, Dotty's wings dried. Patter called out: “Friends, help! We need seven grains of wheat!” The ants came pitter-patter. Dotty laughed: “Seven? I have seven spots too. I'll count! One spot for each grain: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven! Exactly seven!”

benek.say: Seven grains, seven spots, all done!

mech.done: Seven grains in the nest. Just in time!

pages.hint: Carry the grains to the nest!
pages.ask: The ants carried, Dotty counted. Which job could you help with at home?

pages.text: Pitter, patter, pit! The rain began. The wheat was in the nest, nice and dry. But Dotty couldn't fit in the nest! The ants didn't leave her alone. All together, they ran under the big mushroom. Patter smiled: “Together, the load feels lighter!”

pitir.say: Our store is full to the top!

benek.say: Thank you! My wings are nice and dry.

pages.ask: Why didn't the ants leave Dotty alone? Who have you done a job together with?

kazanim: MAB.1 Counting rhythmically and by sight (learning outcome): finds how many objects there are (1–10) by counting; counts the seven grains of wheat by touching them one by one, and counts again while carrying them to the nest (48–60 months adaptation: 1–10).

FAB.1 Making scientific observations of science-related events, facts and situations in daily life: observes and describes the signs of autumn (leaves turning yellow and falling, cooler air, gathering grey clouds) and that a wet wing dries in the sun.

E1.3 Perseverance and Determination (disposition): does not give up when the grain is too heavy; keeps carrying the load, saying 'Step by step, one more step!' (page 3). With the same words, walks with Dotty all the way to the sun.
SDB2.2 Cooperation: shares tasks for a common goal (the ants carry, Dotty counts); asks for help and gives help when needed, and does not leave a friend alone in the rain.
D3 Diligence, D20 Helpfulness: recognises the value of getting ready for winter in advance and of lending each other a hand.
once: Point to the ant on the cover: “How do you think this ant is getting ready for winter?”
Look out of the window or remember: “How do the leaves and the weather change in autumn?”
If you have a picture or a toy ladybird, count the spots on its back together.
sirasi: On the counting page, touch each grain with your finger and count to a rhythm: “One, two, three…” If a grain is skipped or counted twice, smile and count again from the start.
Let the child make the “Heave, ho!” and “Pitter, patter, pit!” sounds; repeat “Step by step, one more step!” together.
On the prediction page, ask about the choice: “Why did you think that?” Both options are good ideas.
Explain the word dew: the tiny drops of water that collect on grass and leaves in the morning.
sonra: After the ordering game, ask the child to retell the story from the beginning in their own words.
Ask: “How did Patter help Dotty? How did Dotty help the ants?”

Information note: Some ants (harvester ants) really do collect seeds and grains of wheat and store them in the nest. Ladybirds spend the winter under log bark or leaves. Mushrooms in nature are not for eating; we only look at them from a distance. Harvester ants (Messor), which also live in Turkey, carry seeds to the nest; you can watch ant trails at the edges of fields together, without touching.
Count five to seven objects together, then draw the same number of dots: “Seven objects, seven dots; they're both the same!”

sinif.materyal: Seven yellow paper balls (grains of wheat), two hoops (field and nest), a red card with seven empty circles drawn on it (Dotty card), round sticky labels
adim: Make one hoop the 'field' and the other the 'nest'. Put the seven yellow paper balls in the field.
The children become ants. Saying “Pitter patter!”, they take turns carrying one grain each.
One child becomes 'Dotty'. Each time a grain enters the nest, they stick a label on one circle on the card and count out loud.
When all seven are done, say “The rain is coming!” Everyone 'shelters' around the nest hoop. Swap roles and play again.
Talk about it: “Was it easier alone or together? Why?”

evSoru: Why did Patter collect wheat before winter came?
What did the ants do for Dotty when the rain started?
Who have you done a job together with at home? How did you feel?

evEtk.d: Cut a ladybird out of paper. Together, collect seven things from around the house (a spoon, a sock, a toy…) into a basket. Each time something goes into the basket, draw a spot on the ladybird. At the end, count the things and the spots separately: are they both seven?

guide.aileNotu: Today we read 'The Ants Get Ready for Winter.' While trying to carry seven grains of wheat to the nest before the rain, Patter the ant helped Dotty the ladybird, whose wings had got wet; then the ants carried and Dotty counted. At home, counting objects together by touching them and giving your child a small job supports counting skills, diligence and cooperation. You can also talk about the Turkish saying 'karınca kararınca' (an ant does what an ant can): everyone helps as much as they are able.
